name: Quantitative evaluation
models: Reported, as of Nov 2026: SIG's Quantitative Evaluation. Seventeen questions in 60 minutes with a calculator, rising from quick expected values to multi-stage Bayes and ruin.
description: This is the reported format of SIG's Quantitative Evaluation, as candidates described it by Nov 2026. You have 17 questions in 60 minutes. A calculator is allowed, but the app has none, so have a basic one ready. The questions start with quick expected values and end with multi-stage Bayes and gambler's ruin. Some take a choice, others a number to three decimal places. A wrong answer scores 0, and you may change answers until you submit. Other reports give 16 questions in 20 minutes; this mock follows the longer one. This is version 1 of 3.

items.title: A die that pays squares
items.question: A fair 6-sided die, faces 1 to 6, pays £ the square of the face shown. What is a fair price to play once?

options.why: You squared the average face, $3.5^2$, instead of averaging the squares.
You priced the face itself, not its square.
You added the squares but did not divide by 6.

feedback.correct: The mean of the squares is $\tfrac{91}{6}$, about £15.17.
feedback.generic: Average the squares of the faces, not the square of the average face.

items.title: Cards of one kind
items.question: You deal 5 cards from a well-shuffled 52-card deck. What is the expected number of hearts among them?

options.why: You gave the chance for one card, not the count over all 5.
You counted the cards that are not hearts.
You used the share of one rank, 1 in 13, instead of one suit, 1 in 4.

feedback.correct: Each card is a heart with chance $\tfrac{1}{4}$, so $5 \times \tfrac{1}{4} = \tfrac{5}{4}$.
feedback.generic: Give each card an indicator for being a heart, then add the chances.

explain.text: Card $j$ is a heart with chance $\tfrac{13}{52} = \tfrac{1}{4}$, whatever the other cards are. Linearity adds the 5 chances: $\tfrac{5}{4}$. The cards are dependent, but an expectation does not care.

items.title: A game with a fee
items.question: You pay £3 to roll a fair six-sided die. You receive £ the face if it is even, and nothing otherwise. What is your expected profit per game?

options.why: You counted only the fee and left out the payout.
You paid out the face on every roll: $3.5 - 3$.
You found the expected payout and forgot the £3 fee.

feedback.correct: The payout averages £2.00, so the profit is −£1.00 a game.
feedback.generic: Average the payout over all six faces, then take off the fee.

explain.text: $E[\text{payout}] = \tfrac{2 + 4 + 6}{6} = 2$, so the profit is $2 - 3 = -1$. Check: half the rolls pay, averaging 4, so $\tfrac12 \times 4 - 3 = -1$.

items.title: Pairs of heads
items.question: You toss a fair coin 10 times. Count each place where two heads stand side by side, overlaps included: HHH holds two. What is the expected count?

options.why: You counted 10 places for a pair, but 10 tosses have only 9.
You gave each place chance $\tfrac12$, but both tosses must be heads.
You split the tosses into separate pairs and missed the overlapping ones.

feedback.correct: There are 9 places, each with chance $\tfrac14$: $9 \times \tfrac14 = \tfrac{9}{4} = 2.25$.
feedback.generic: Give each neighbouring pair of tosses an indicator, then add the chances.

explain.text: Indicator $I_j$ marks heads at tosses $j$ and $j + 1$, for $j = 1$ to $9$. Each has $E[I_j] = \tfrac14$, so the count averages $\tfrac{9}{4} = 2.25$. Overlapping pairs are dependent, but linearity does not care.

items.title: At least one six
items.question: You roll a fair six-sided die 4 times. What is the chance of at least one six? Give three decimal places.

widget.label: Chance of at least one six

feedback.generic: Find the chance of no six at all, then take it from 1.

byKey.times: You added $\tfrac16$ 4 times, which counts rolls with two sixes twice.
byKey.none: That is the chance of no six. Take it from 1.
byKey.one: That is the chance for a single roll.

explain.text: No six in 4 rolls has chance $(\tfrac56)^4 = \tfrac{625}{1296}$. So at least one six has chance $\tfrac{671}{1296} \approx 0.518$. Check: of the 1,296 equally likely outcomes, 671 hold a six.

items.title: Two cards, at least one
items.question: You draw two cards from a well-shuffled 52-card deck, without replacement. At least one is an ace. What is the chance that both are aces?

options.why: You took the first card as an ace, but "at least one" could be either card.
You found the chance of two aces before using the condition.
You gave the chance that a single card is an ace.

feedback.correct: 6 pairs of aces out of 198 pairs that hold one: $\tfrac{1}{33}$.
feedback.generic: Count unordered pairs: two aces, over pairs with at least one.

explain.text: There are $\binom{52}{2} = 1{,}326$ pairs, and $\binom{48}{2} = 1{,}128$ hold no ace. So 198 pairs hold at least one, and $\binom{4}{2} = 6$ hold two. The chance is $\tfrac{6}{198} = \tfrac{1}{33}$.

items.title: Exactly so many heads
items.question: You toss a fair coin 6 times. What is the chance of exactly 3 heads?

options.why: You priced one order, such as HHHTTT, but there are $\binom{6}{3} = 20$ of them.
You gave the share of heads, $3$ in $6$, as a chance.
You found the chance of at least 3 heads.

feedback.generic: Count the orders with 3 heads, then multiply by the chance of one order.

explain.text: Each sequence of 6 tosses has chance $\tfrac{1}{64}$. Exactly 3 heads happens in $\binom{6}{3} = 20$ of them, so the chance is $\tfrac{20}{64} = \tfrac{5}{16}$.

items.title: The heavy coin
items.question: You have 10 coins that look the same. One is heavier and the rest weigh the same. Using a balance scale, what is the fewest weighings that always finds the heavy coin?

options.why: You split the coins in two each time, which wastes the balanced outcome.
You weighed the coins one pair at a time.
You set one coin against each other coin in turn.

feedback.correct: Each weighing splits the suspects three ways, and $3^{2} < 10 \le 3^{3}$.
feedback.generic: A weighing has three outcomes, so split the coins into three groups.

explain.text: Each weighing has three outcomes: left heavy, right heavy or balanced. So $k$ weighings can single out one coin among at most $3^k$, and $3^{2} = 9 < 10 \le 27$. Put equal groups in the pans and the rest aside, none above 9 coins, then repeat on the suspects.

items.title: A positive test
items.question: A condition affects 1% of people. A test catches 95% of true cases and flags 5% of healthy people by mistake. A person tests positive. What is the chance they have the condition? Give three decimal places.

feedback.generic: Picture 10,000 people and count the true and the false positives.

byKey.hit: That is the chance of a positive given the condition, the wrong way round.
byKey.base: You kept the base rate and ignored the test.

explain.text: In 10,000 people, 100 have it and 95 of them test positive. Of the 9,900 without it, 495 test positive. So $P = \tfrac{95}{95 + 495} = \tfrac{19}{118} \approx 0.161$.

items.title: Waiting for a pattern
items.question: You toss a fair coin until HH first appears in consecutive tosses. What is the expected number of tosses?

options.why: You took one over the chance of HH, which is the gap between repeats, not the first wait.
You waited for H, 2 tosses, and assumed the next toss obliges.
You gave the shortest possible wait, not the average.

feedback.correct: Solving the state equations gives 6 tosses.
feedback.generic: Write one equation per state of progress, from scratch to one short of the pattern.

explain.text: Let $a$ be the wait from scratch and $b$ the wait after one head. Then $a = 1 + \tfrac12 b + \tfrac12 a$ and $b = 1 + \tfrac12 a$, since a tail restarts. So $a = 2 + b = 3 + \tfrac12 a$, giving $a = 6$.

items.title: Roll again or keep
items.question: A fair 6-sided die, faces 1 to 6, pays £ the face. After the first roll you may reroll once, and you must keep the last face rolled. Under the best rule, what is the game worth?

options.why: You never rerolled, so you took the plain average.
You kept only 5 or more, but 4 beats the £3.50 a reroll is worth.
You took the largest face rolled, but a reroll throws the old face away.

feedback.correct: Keep 4, 5 or 6, because a reroll is worth only £3.50.
feedback.generic: Work backwards: keep a face only if it beats the value of rolling again.

explain.text: A reroll is worth £3.50, so keep any face above 3.5. The value is $\tfrac{4 + 5 + 6}{6} + \tfrac{3}{6} \times 3.5 = 4.25$.

items.title: One face of two dice
items.question: You roll two fair 6-sided dice, faces 1 to 6. What is the expected value of the larger face? If they tie, that face counts. Give three decimal places.

feedback.generic: Find $P(\max \le k)$ first: both dice must be at most $k$.

byKey.one: That is the mean of one die; the larger of two is pulled up.
byKey.other: That is the expected smaller face.
byKey.distinct: You left out the doubles, which are as likely as any other ordered pair.

explain.text: Both dice must be at most $k$, so $P(\max \le k) = (\tfrac{k}{6})^2$ and $P(\max = k) = \tfrac{2k - 1}{36}$. Then $E = \tfrac{1 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot 3 + \dots + 6 \cdot 11}{36} = \tfrac{161}{36} \approx 4.472$. Check: $E[\max] + E[\min] = 7$, and $E[\min] = \tfrac{91}{36}$.

items.title: The two-headed coin
items.question: A bag holds 3 fair coins and one coin with two heads. You draw a coin at random and toss it 3 times. It shows 3 heads. What is the chance it is the two-headed coin?

options.why: You kept the prior $\tfrac{1}{4}$ and ignored the 3 heads.
You gave the two kinds of coin equal priors, but fair coins outnumber it 3 to 1.
You took one minus a fair coin's chance of 3 heads.

feedback.generic: Weigh each kind of coin by its prior times its chance of 3 heads.

explain.text: Prior odds are $1 : 3$, and 3 heads are $2^3 = 8$ times likelier with the two-headed coin. Posterior odds are $8 : 3$, so $P = \tfrac{8}{11}$. Check: $\tfrac{1/4}{1/4 + 3/4 \times 1/8} = \tfrac{8}{11}$.

items.title: Two positive tests
items.question: A condition affects 1% of people. A test catches 95% of true cases and flags 5% of healthy people. One person takes it twice, with independent results, and is positive both times. What is the chance they have the condition? Give three decimal places.

feedback.generic: Each positive multiplies the odds by $\tfrac{95}{5}$.

byKey.once: That uses one positive only. Update the odds again for the second.
byKey.square: You squared the hit rate and ignored the false positives.

explain.text: Prior odds are $\tfrac{1}{99}$, and each positive multiplies them by $\tfrac{95}{5} = 19$. Two positives give odds $\tfrac{361}{99}$, so $P = \tfrac{361}{460} \approx 0.785$. Check: $\tfrac{0.01 \times 0.95^2}{0.01 \times 0.95^2 + 0.99 \times 0.05^2}$ gives the same.

items.title: How long a fair game lasts
items.question: You start with £3 and bet £1 at a time on a fair coin. You stop when you reach £0 or £10. What is the expected number of bets?

options.why: You counted the steps to £10 as if every bet were a win.
You multiplied 3 by 10; the formula uses the distances to both ends.
You squared the distance to £10 and ignored the floor at £0.

explain.text: The duration $D_k$ satisfies $D_k = 1 + \tfrac12(D_{k-1} + D_{k+1})$, with $D_0 = D_{10} = 0$. Its solution is $D_k = k(10 - k)$, so $D_3 = 21$. Check: $1 + \tfrac12(D_2 + D_4) = 1 + \tfrac12(16 + 24) = 21$.

items.title: Ruin with an edge
items.question: You start with £2. Each £1 bet wins with chance 0.6, independently. You stop when you reach £0 or £5. What is the chance you reach £5? Give three decimal places.

feedback.generic: Use $P_i = \tfrac{1 - r^i}{1 - r^N}$, where $r = \tfrac{q}{p}$ is the losing odds.

byKey.fair: That is the fair-coin answer $\tfrac{2}{5}$, but the edge is on your side.
byKey.streak: You needed 3 wins in a row, but losses can be won back.
byKey.one: That is the chance of winning a single bet.

explain.text: $P_k$ solves $P_k = pP_{k+1} + qP_{k-1}$ with $P_0 = 0$ and $P_{5} = 1$, so $P_k = \tfrac{1 - r^k}{1 - r^{5}}$ with $r = \tfrac{q}{p} = \tfrac{2}{3}$. So $P_2 = \tfrac{1 - (2/3)^2}{1 - (2/3)^{5}} = \tfrac{135}{211} \approx 0.640$. Check: shooting $P_{k+1} = (P_k - qP_{k-1})/p$ from $P_0 = 0$ gives the same.

items.title: Which coin got you there
items.question: A coin is either fair or lands heads with chance three in four, each equally likely. You start with £1 and bet £1 on heads at each toss. You stop at £0 or £3. You reach £3. What is the chance the coin is the biased one? Give three decimal places.

feedback.generic: Find each coin's chance of reaching £3, then use Bayes with equal priors.

byKey.stage: That is the chance of reaching £3. Now condition on having reached it.
byKey.biased: That is the biased coin's chance of reaching £3, not the posterior.
byKey.prior: You kept the prior and ignored that you reached £3.

explain.text: From £1 a fair coin reaches £3 with chance $\tfrac13$, and the biased one with $\tfrac{1 - r}{1 - r^3} = \tfrac{9}{13}$, where $r = \tfrac{1}{3}$. The equal priors cancel, so $P = \tfrac{9/13}{1/3 + 9/13} = \tfrac{27}{40} \approx 0.675$.
